root.note: Probably ‘the thing that belongs to a bird’, from *h₂éwis ‘bird’, the word behind Latin avis. Latin ovum and Greek ōión come from the same root.

stages.meaning: egg, used in the north of England

history: Old English had its own word for egg: ǣg, plural ǣgru. In Middle English it was ey, with the plural eyren. In the north of England, where many Vikings had settled, people said egg, from Old Norse. For a while both words were used. In 1490 the printer William Caxton told a famous story. Some merchants on a ship on the Thames stopped in Kent and asked a woman for ‘egges’. She answered that she did not speak French. Then another man asked for ‘eyren’, and she understood. Which word, Caxton asked, should a printer use? In the end, the northern egg won. Both words go back to the same old root as Latin ovum and Greek ōión.
historyEinfach: In old English, egg was ey. Two eggs were eyren. In the north of England, people said egg. This was a Viking word. In 1490, a man wrote a funny story. Some men asked a woman for ‘egges’. She did not understand. She thought it was French! Then a man asked for ‘eyren’, and she understood. Later, everybody said egg.

elsewhere.text: German kept the form without g: Ei, plural Eier. It looks just like southern Middle English ey, eyren, the word the woman in Caxton's story knew.
French œuf comes from Latin ōvum, a distant cousin of egg. English borrowed from the Latin side too: oval means ‘egg-shaped’.
